holidays.name: National Chocolate-Covered Cherry Day
holidays.description: A day to celebrate the sweet-meets-tart candy with a gooey liquid center, a little burst of syrupy surprise inside a snappy chocolate shell.
holidays.origin: Like many American food days, it is an unofficial observance that appears in food-holiday calendars. The candy itself relies on an enzyme called invertase, which turns the fondant around the cherry into liquid after the chocolate is applied.
holidays.funFact: The cherry is surrounded by solid fondant when dipped in chocolate. Invertase mixed into the fondant breaks down the sugar over days or weeks, which is how the liquid center forms.

holidays.name: Festival of Sleep Day
holidays.description: A day devoted to getting back the rest you lost during the holiday season, with naps, extra-long snoozes, and zero guilt about staying in bed.
holidays.origin: It is an unofficial observance on quirky-holiday calendars, created to give worn-out people permission to recover from the busy holidays and start the new year well rested.
holidays.funFact: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has described insufficient sleep as a public health problem, with about one in three U.S. adults regularly not getting enough.

holidays.name: J.R.R. Tolkien Day
holidays.description: Fans of Middle-earth celebrate the birthday of the author of The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings with second breakfasts, readings, and elvish quotes.
holidays.origin: John Ronald Reuel Tolkien was born on January 3, 1892, in Bloemfontein, South Africa. Fans marked the date as a tribute to the man who built an entire fantasy world and its languages.
holidays.funFact: Tolkien was a professor of Anglo-Saxon at Oxford and invented several languages, including Quenya and Sindarin, before he wrote the stories that were set in the world where they were spoken.

holidays.name: Drinking Straw Day
holidays.description: A salute to the humble tube that has made sipping easier for generations, from fancy cocktails to milkshakes.
holidays.origin: The date is tied to Marvin Stone, who patented the paper drinking straw on January 3, 1888. He had grown tired of rye grass straws leaving a grassy taste in his mint juleps, so he wrapped paper around a pencil and glued it.
holidays.funFact: Marvin Stone's paper straws were coated in paraffin wax so they would not get soggy, and the very first drinking straws date back thousands of years to Sumerian gold and lapis lazuli tubes used to drink beer.

holidays.name: Fruitcake Toss Day
holidays.description: A day when people fling leftover holiday fruitcakes with enthusiasm, in contests of distance and accuracy.
holidays.origin: Fruitcake Toss celebrations started as a way to dispose of unwanted fruitcake gifts after the holidays. Manitou Springs, Colorado, hosts a famous Great Fruitcake Toss every January with cakes launched by catapults, cannons, and slingshots.
holidays.funFact: Fruitcake is so durable that a fruitcake from Robert Falcon Scott's 1910 Antarctic expedition was found over a century later and was reportedly still in edible-looking condition.
